Orchestrating traffic with data
Roadworks, a busy evening rush hour, an accident, or someone hitting the brakes… any of these events can cause congestion and affect the rest of the road network in no time at all. Hans van Lint uses smart models to predict traffic flow, enabling traffic managers to orchestrate the flow. “If you don’t push the right buttons at the right time, it’s mayhem.”
reading time: min
In-depth study underpins smart offshore windturbines
Lack of suitable space means more offshore turbines will be built in deeper water, where their foundations are subjected to strong wave action. Oriol Colomés and Alexander Heinlein of TU Delft are working on designs for new monopiles able to withstand extreme conditions. Simulations are helping them to find out what will make the foundations stronger.
reading time: 6 min
Taking the plunge on a floating future
The floating city is no hypermodern illusion. Even today, there are numerous examples of housing and infrastructure built on water. What would this floating future look like? Can it meet high expectations, such as adapting to sea level rise and creating more space for housing? Four researchers from TU Delft discuss the possibilities of floating construction.
Asphalt to dream of
Many Dutch highways are due for maintenance, but heavy traffic, high costs and sustainability requirements are making it difficult to determine which should be tackled first. Katerina Varveri is developing ways to make asphalt more sustainable and longer lasting. Using smart measurement methods, she can identify which roads are first in line for an environmentally friendly makeover. From smart planning to circular materials: the future of road infrastructure is taking shape here.
reading time: 5 min
Melting ice, rising ground: a new perspective on sea-level predictions
Melting of the Antarctic ice sheet is expected to become the dominant contributor to sea-level rise, potentially adding eight metres by the year 2300. But as the ice sheet thins, the ground beneath slowly rises, somewhat reducing ice loss. Caroline van Calcar’s detailed modelling of the interplay between ice melt and ground uplift improves the accuracy of sea-level rise predictions.
reading time: min
How to keep a cool head in an increasingly hot environment
Handling heat stress is just one of the many challenges cities are faced with as the effects of climate change and population growth are taking their toll on the living environment. Temperatures may vary within a single street, making this a complex issue. Researchers and students from different disciplines have been enlisting the help of citizens - and their backyard - to measure the effects of heat stress in an urban environment to help them devise ways of combating it.
reading time: 11 min
Buildings that fix themselves
Imagine if cracks in brick walls could heal by themselves – with a little help from bacteria. This “self-healing” technology has already been proven to work in concrete, but could it be applied to masonry as well? Researcher Belen Gaggero is testing this very possibility, and her results are promising so far.

Discover how TU Delft research in geothermal energy, design, and human behaviour drives the heat transition towards a gas-free future.
